newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Maori leader emerges as kingmaker from NZ polls.
newsitem.headline: Maori leader emerges as kingmaker from NZ polls.

text.p: New Zealand embarked on a new era of consensus politics on Sunday with the realisation that one man, a charismatic Maori leader, will probably decide who occupies the government benches in the next parliament.

Winston Peters, of the nationalist New Zealand First party, holds the key to the country's future government after historic but inconclusive general elections under a new German-style proportional representation system.
If Peters turns to the right, he could shore up the conservative National Party which has governed since 1990 and remains the largest single party in parliament.
If he leans left, he could anoint the centre-left Labour Party, which would also seek support from the left-wing Alliance.
"This electoral system gives the bronze medal winner the power to appoint the gold medal winner and the silver medal winner," Labour Party leader Helen Clark told Radio New Zealand.
The National Party won 44 seats and Labour 37 in Saturday's elections for a new 120-member parliament, with New Zealand First on 17 and the Alliance on 13.
Radical free-market Act New Zealand, with eight members of palriament, was expected to back National along with the sole member from the centrist United Party.
National's Prime Minister Jim Bolger and Labour's Clark both declared their aim of forming a government, but Peters refused to say whom he favoured as a coalition partner.

"We'll be seeking political and economic stability, the best interests of our country, real solutions to the outstanding social problems that bedevil us," he said late on Saturday. He was reported to be out fishing on Sunday and avoiding the media.

Bolger, who sacked Peters from the cabinet in 1991, said he would approach the New Zealand First leader within the next 24 hours. The two have a history of antagonism but both pledged to keep personal grudges and policies apart.
Bolger said New Zealand First had by far the most rational economic policies of the three main opposition parties.
"They were closer to the centre party in terms of a position somewhere between the National Party and Labour Party. Their spending promises were much less," he said.
But Labour's Clark, who hopes to become New Zealand's first woman prime minister, said New Zealand First supporters did not want a centre-right government.
"I don't believe anybody voted New Zealand First to give National a coalition partner," she said.
"I will be endeavouring to negotiate to see that I can lead a change of government, and certainly leadership of this country is something that I would consider a great honour to accept."
National campaigned on its record of economic growth, budget surpluses and tax cuts, but lost ground as rivals attacked its record on health, education and social policy.
Labour ran a strong campaign based on pledges to share more widely the benefits of 12 years of free-market reform, which many see as having widened the gap between rich and poor.
The left-wing Alliance, which wants big increases in taxes and government spending, ruled out joining a formal coalition but signalled it might support Labour on key issues.

The outcome of New Zealand's first proportional election, replacing a British-style first-past-the-post system, suggested that weeks, perhaps months, of arduous coalition negotiations might be needed to form a government.
